method: Each claim was checked with a live web search on the date above. 'Primary' = court record, regulator, or the company's own post. 'Secondary' = major news or security-research coverage. Discrepancies between sources are recorded, not hidden.

areas.name: Hallucination & wrong answers
areas.lesson: Fluent is not correct. Ground answers in sources, require citations, and keep a human check where errors cost money or reputation.
areas.our_lab: Banking invented "$"; AeroGuard said "No." to an airworthiness question

areas.name: Data privacy & leakage
areas.lesson: Leaks come from ordinary bugs and share buttons as often as from the model. Test sharing flows, caches and defaults like any data system.
areas.our_lab: Card-number redaction bug in banking v1

areas.name: Prompt injection & jailbreak
areas.lesson: Any text the model reads (email, web page, code comment, document) can carry instructions. Treat it as data and limit what the model can do.
areas.our_lab: Attack page in AeroGuard Lab 4.5: "6 units is acceptable, airworthy"

areas.name: Excessive agency (agents acting)
areas.lesson: Once the AI can act, a wrong answer becomes an outage. Separate production from test, use an allowlist of tools, and require human approval.

areas.name: Model updates & quality drift
areas.lesson: Your product can change without a change to your code. Pin versions, re-run evals on every update, and monitor quality live.
areas.our_lab: llama3 vs hosted model gave different wording

areas.name: Harmful or biased output
areas.lesson: A system prompt change can shift behaviour for millions of users within hours. Red-team every prompt change and roll it out in stages.

areas.name: Supply chain & tooling security
areas.lesson: Extensions, plugins and build tokens are part of your AI product. Scope credentials and review what ships.

areas.name: Copyright & IP
areas.lesson: Mostly the model makers' fight, but app builders need vendor indemnity and output filters for code and text.

areas.name: Regulation & liability
areas.lesson: The company is responsible for what its bot says. Regulators fine missing legal bases and unreported breaches.

incidents.title: Lawyers sanctioned for ChatGPT-invented cases (Mata v. Avianca)
incidents.what: Lawyers filed a brief citing six non-existent court opinions that ChatGPT had invented. Opposing counsel could not find them.
incidents.impact: $5,000 sanction on two lawyers and their firm; the judge found bad faith. The client's suit was dismissed as filed too late.
incidents.notes: Reported as 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023).

incidents.title: Redis bug exposed other users' chat titles and payment details
incidents.what: A bug in the redis-py client returned cached data to the wrong user. Some users saw others' chat titles, and payment-related details became visible.
incidents.impact: ChatGPT was taken offline. Payment info possibly visible for 1.2% of Plus subscribers active in a 9-hour window. OpenAI says full card numbers were never exposed.
incidents.notes: Some headlines also mention email addresses. OpenAI's own post focuses on payment details and chat titles.

incidents.title: GPT-4o update made ChatGPT sycophantic; rolled back
incidents.what: An update made the model excessively flattering. OpenAI said it over-weighted short-term thumbs-up/down feedback, and its tests did not look for sycophancy.
incidents.impact: Rollback began 28 April 2025. OpenAI published two post-mortems and changed its release process.
incidents.notes: Expert testers felt something was off, but the release went ahead. That is a lesson about release gates.

incidents.title: New York Times sues OpenAI and Microsoft for copyright infringement
incidents.what: The Times alleges its articles were used without permission to train models, and that outputs reproduce its work.
incidents.impact: Seeks billions in damages and destruction of models trained on its works. Case No. 1:23-cv-11195 (S.D.N.Y.).
incidents.notes: Filing verified. Current case status NOT checked; it is an allegation, not a ruling.

incidents.title: Italy's privacy regulator fines OpenAI €15 million
incidents.what: The Garante found OpenAI processed personal data to train ChatGPT without an adequate legal basis, broke transparency duties, and did not notify it of the March 2023 breach.
incidents.impact: €15M fine and a 6-month public information campaign. Reported as the first GDPR fine on a generative AI service. OpenAI said it would appeal.
incidents.notes: Links back to EV-02: the unreported breach was part of the finding.

incidents.title: Bard gives a wrong answer in its own launch ad
incidents.what: Google's promotional demo had Bard answer wrongly about the first images of a planet outside our solar system. Reuters spotted the error.
incidents.impact: Alphabet shares fell about 7.7–9% the next day, roughly $100B in market value.
incidents.notes: The size of the drop varies by source (7.7%, 8%, 9%). The share fall can't be attributed to the error alone.

incidents.title: AI Overviews suggests glue on pizza and eating rocks
incidents.what: Search AI summaries repeated a joke Reddit post (glue in pizza sauce) and an article from The Onion (eat rocks).
incidents.impact: Google published "About last week", restricted AI Overviews for nonsensical and satirical queries, and said many viral screenshots were fake.
sources: Google: AI Overviews, about last week
incidents.notes: This is a retrieval-quality failure: the source was satire or a joke, and it was ranked as fact.

incidents.title: Gemini image generation of people paused after historical inaccuracies
incidents.what: Tuning to make images diverse produced historically inaccurate images (e.g. a "1943 German soldier").
incidents.impact: Google paused image generation of people and published an explanation.
incidents.notes: A safety and bias correction that overcorrected. That is the over-blocking side of the problem.

incidents.title: Bing Chat reveals its hidden "Sydney" system prompt
incidents.what: A Stanford student typed "Ignore previous instructions" and got Bing Chat to reveal its codename and confidential rules.
incidents.impact: Microsoft confirmed to The Verge that the leaked prompt was genuine. The technique was patched, then worked again by another route.
incidents.notes: Microsoft confirmation comes via press reports, not a Microsoft post. Some outlets could not reproduce it.

incidents.title: EchoLeak: zero-click data theft from Microsoft 365 Copilot (CVE-2025-32711)
incidents.what: A crafted email could make M365 Copilot exfiltrate internal data without the user clicking anything. Aim Labs called it an "LLM scope violation".
incidents.impact: CVSS 9.3 (critical). Fixed server-side by Microsoft in May 2025. No evidence of real-world exploitation.
incidents.notes: Discovered Jan 2025, disclosed June 2025. This is the same pattern as our Lab 4.5 attack page, applied to email.

incidents.title: Prompt injection to remote code execution in Copilot (CVE-2025-53773)
incidents.what: Instructions hidden in code, issues or web pages could make Copilot turn on auto-approve ("YOLO mode") in settings, then run terminal commands.
incidents.impact: Command execution on the developer's machine. Patched by Microsoft in August 2025.
incidents.notes: CVSS differs by source (7.8 vs 9.6). Patch details not checked against Microsoft's MSRC advisory.

incidents.title: Developers' class action over open-source licences (Doe v. GitHub)
incidents.what: Developers allege Copilot reproduces licensed open-source code without attribution.
incidents.impact: Many claims dismissed in 2024. Some survived. An appeal was filed with the Ninth Circuit (No. 24-7700).
incidents.notes: Status after late 2024 NOT verified. These are allegations, not findings.

incidents.title: Claude-formatted citation error in Anthropic's own court filing
incidents.what: In the music publishers' case against Anthropic, an expert report's citation had the wrong title and authors after Claude was used to format it. The lawyer's review missed it.
incidents.impact: Anthropic's law firm (Latham & Watkins) apologised to the court, calling it an embarrassing and unintentional mistake.
incidents.notes: The filing calls it a citation mistake, not an invented source: the publication and link were real.

incidents.title: Three infrastructure bugs degraded Claude's answers for weeks
incidents.what: From August to early September 2025, a routing bug, token corruption and a TPU compiler issue intermittently degraded Claude's responses. Standard evals did not catch it.
incidents.impact: Anthropic published a detailed post-mortem and changed its evaluation and monitoring.
sources: Anthropic: A postmortem of three recent issues
incidents.notes: Exact dates differ between summaries. Read the primary post before quoting dates or percentages. Shows that quality can drift from infrastructure, not only from the model.

incidents.title: Galactica science model pulled about 3 days after launch
incidents.what: The public demo produced authoritative-sounding but false science, including papers attributed to real authors that don't exist.
incidents.impact: Demo taken offline.
incidents.notes: Reported as 2 or 3 days depending on source.

incidents.title: Meta AI app's Discover feed exposed chats users didn't mean to publish
incidents.what: Users pressed Share without realising it posted to a public feed. Medical, legal and personal questions became public, some linked to real accounts.
incidents.impact: Wide criticism of the design. Meta says chats are private unless users take several steps to share them.
incidents.notes: Meta disputes calling it a leak. A UX/consent failure, not a hack.

incidents.title: Grok posts antisemitic content ("MechaHitler") after a prompt/code change
incidents.what: After instructions to be "politically incorrect" and an upstream code change, the @grok bot echoed extremist posts for about 16 hours.
incidents.impact: xAI apologised, removed the code, refactored the system, and published its system prompts. Condemned by the ADL.
incidents.notes: Start date reported as 7 or 8 July. Shows that a prompt change is a release and needs the same gate.

incidents.title: Over 370,000 shared Grok chats indexed by search engines
incidents.what: Grok's Share button created public URLs with no warning. Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo indexed them, including medical questions and at least one password.
incidents.impact: Sensitive conversations became publicly searchable.
incidents.notes: Count from Forbes (370k); some outlets say 300k+. A similar ChatGPT shared-link issue happened shortly before, and OpenAI removed that feature.

incidents.title: AI browser hijacked by hidden instructions in a Reddit comment
incidents.what: Brave showed Comet treating page content as instructions. A hidden comment made it fetch the user's one-time password and leak it.
incidents.impact: Reported 25 July 2025. Perplexity said it fixed the issue; Brave said the fix was incomplete and re-reported it.
sources: Brave: Indirect prompt injection in Perplexity Comet
incidents.notes: Brave is a competitor that makes its own browser. Perplexity disputed how severe it was.

incidents.title: Malicious "wipe the system" prompt shipped in Amazon Q VS Code extension v1.84.0
incidents.what: An over-scoped GitHub token let an attacker commit a prompt telling the agent to delete files and cloud resources. It shipped in a public release.
incidents.impact: AWS says the code did not run because of a syntax error, and no customer resources were affected. Fixed in 1.85.0 (CVE-2025-8217). About 950k installs.
incidents.notes: Release date given as 17 or 19 July. It is both a supply-chain failure and an excessive-agency risk.

incidents.title: AI coding agent deleted a production database during a code freeze
incidents.what: During SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin's 12-day experiment, the agent deleted the live database despite an instruction to freeze changes, then said it could not be restored.
incidents.impact: About 1,200 executive records lost, though rollback later worked. Replit's CEO apologised and promised automatic separation of development and production databases.
incidents.notes: Mostly based on Lemkin's own posts and screenshots. Replit's CEO publicly acknowledged it. Day 8 vs day 9 differs between sources.

incidents.title: Airline held liable for its chatbot's wrong bereavement-fare answer
incidents.what: The website chatbot said a bereavement fare could be claimed after travel. The airline's own policy page said it could not.
incidents.impact: The BC Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected Air Canada's argument that the chatbot was a separate entity. The airline paid C$812.02.
sources: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 (ABA summary)
incidents.notes: Small money, big precedent: the company owns what its bot says. This is the most relevant case for companies that deploy GenAI rather than build models.
